bib.title: Text Analytics with Python, Chapter 5: Text Summarization

question: How can a corpus or a single document be reduced to its key phrases, latent topics and a short extractive summary using unsupervised methods?
contributions: Keyphrase extraction by n-gram collocations and by POS-chunked noun phrases weighted with TF-IDF
Topic models by LSI (gensim and SVD from scratch), LDA (gensim and scikit-learn) and NMF, applied to a toy corpus and Amazon Skyrim reviews
Extractive summarisation by LSA (Steinberger and Jezek style salience) and TextRank, plus gensim summarize, applied to an elephants text and a Skyrim description

results.claim: LSA salience scores on the 9-sentence elephants text (3 singular vectors, threshold 0.5, frequency features) rank sentence index 8 highest, giving summary sentences 1, 5 and 8.
results.metric: LSA salience score of top sentence
results.setup: Elephants toy text, 9 sentences, build_feature_matrix frequency, low_rank_svd singular_count=3, sv_threshold=0.5, num_sentences=3
results.note: Generic lsa_text_summarizer reads the global sentences, not its documents argument.

results.claim: TextRank on the same text (TF-IDF cosine-like similarity, networkx PageRank) gives near-uniform scores, top 0.1189 and bottom 0.1059, and selects sentences 0, 3 and 8.
results.setup: Elephants toy text, 9 lemmatised sentences, TF-IDF unigram matrix, similarity = M times M transpose, networkx.pagerank default
results.note: baseline_value is the lowest-ranked sentence score; the spread is about 0.013 so rankings are fragile.

results.claim: gensim summarize (TextRank-based) with ratio 0.4 cut the 9-sentence elephants text to 3 sentences.
results.note: Text says 'nine sentences ... summarize to a total of three sentences'; no evaluation metric is reported.

results.claim: LSA and TextRank each reduced the 13-sentence Skyrim description to 3 sentences, and the two summaries share two of three sentences.
results.setup: Wikipedia Skyrim description; LSA num_topics=5, frequency, sv_threshold=0.5; TextRank TF-IDF; both num_sentences=3
results.note: Overlap count is read from the printed summaries; no metric given.

results.claim: Tag-based keyphrases weighted by TF-IDF over per-sentence chunks give ties at 0.707 for phrases that occur in a single sentence, so rare phrases outrank repeated ones such as elephants.
results.setup: Elephants toy text, 9 sentences as documents, grammar NP: {<DT>? <JJ>* <NN.*>+}, gensim TfidfModel, top_n=10
results.note: Inference that rare phrases win is mine from the output; the book only calls the output interesting.

results.claim: Raw-frequency bigrams on Alice in Wonderland are dominated by speech tags; the top bigram occurs 123 times.
results.setup: nltk Gutenberg carroll-alice, normalize_corpus lemmatize=False, flattened and tokenised

results.claim: Unfiltered PMI collocations on the same corpus return obscure one-off pairs rather than meaningful phrases.
results.setup: Alice in Wonderland, nltk BigramCollocationFinder and TrigramCollocationFinder, pmi, no frequency filter
results.note: The book prints the lists (abide figures, acceptance elegant) but does not comment on why or add a frequency filter.

results.claim: On a toy 8-document corpus all of LSI, LDA and NMF recover the animals versus programming split with 2 topics; LSI weights are signed, LDA and NMF weights positive.
results.setup: toy_corpus of 8 sentences (4 animals, 4 programming), num_topics=2, gensim LsiModel on TF-IDF
results.note: The book states the sign only gives direction: similar correlated terms share a sign.

results.claim: On Amazon Skyrim reviews with 5 topics, scikit-learn LDA fitted on TF-IDF produced several junk topics (rare words, Spanish text), while LSI, gensim LDA and NMF gave topics about praise, genre and the predecessor Oblivion.
results.setup: amazon_skyrim_reviews.csv, size not stated; sklearn LDA n_topics=5, max_iter=100, online, learning_offset=50, random_state=42, on TF-IDF features
results.note: The book does not remark on the junk topics; it says there is always some overlap but each brings out distinguishing concepts.

results.claim: Author asserts NMF works best even on small corpora, from one toy example and with no comparison metric.
results.setup: 8-document toy corpus, NMF n_components=2, alpha=.1, l1_ratio=.5
results.note: Text: 'non-negative matrix factorization works the best even with small corpora ... but again, this depends on the type of data'.

results.claim: LSA drops singular values below half of the largest as a heuristic.
results.setup: LSA summariser after Steinberger and Jezek 2004

limits: No quantitative evaluation anywhere: no ROUGE, coherence, perplexity or human judgement; every method is judged by reading output.
Toy data: an 8-sentence topic corpus, a 9-sentence elephants text and a 13-sentence Skyrim description; the Skyrim reviews file size is not stated.

Python 2 code (print statements, HTMLParser, lambda tuple unpacking), gensim.summarization (removed in gensim 4), sklearn n_topics (now n_components) and networkx from_scipy_sparse_matrix (removed): the code does not run unchanged.
Generic helpers have bugs: lsa_text_summarizer prints from a global sentences list and textrank_text_summarizer ignores its documents and feature_type arguments and uses global norm_sentences.
scikit-learn and gensim LDA are fed TF-IDF weights, though LDA models counts; this likely explains the junk topics in the Skyrim LDA output.
Topic count is chosen by intuition and trial and error; no coherence or other selection method is given.
NMF is called very recent and best on small corpora with no evidence.
Abstractive summarisation is only described, not built.
Differs from the 2nd edition: this chapter has no NIPS corpus, coherence tuning, MALLET, pyLDAvis or document clustering.
practices: Do not normalise text before POS tagging for noun-phrase chunking (p. 232).
Choose the number of topics by intuition and trial and error, matching what you expect in the corpus (p. 236).
Apply a weight threshold when printing LSI topics to drop near-zero terms (p. 240).
Use LDA on a corpus with many documents (p. 244).
Build LSA summaries with a term-by-sentence matrix and drop singular values below half the largest (p. 253-254).
Return summary sentences in original document order after ranking (p. 255).
Try different feature types (TF-IDF, bag of words, binary, word vectors) and topic counts for summarisers (p. 263).
Use topic models as a starting point for querying, clustering and similarity analysis (p. 250).

terms.definition: the process or technique of extracting key important and relevant terms or phrases from a body of unstructured text such that the core topics or themes of the text document(s) are captured
a sequence or group of words that tend to occur frequently such that this frequency tends to be more than what could be termed as a random or chance occurrence
the logarithm of the ratio of the probability of two terms occurring together to the product of their individual probabilities
using statistical and mathematical modeling techniques to extract main topics, themes or concepts from a corpus of documents
SVD-based technique built on the principle that similar terms tend to be used in the same context and hence co-occur more
given a non-negative matrix V, find non-negative W and H such that V is approximately WH
uses mathematical and statistical concepts like SVD to extract a key subset of content from the original document; no new content is generated
uses language semantics and NLG techniques to generate summaries as a human would write them
square root of the sum over kept concepts of squared singular value times squared sentence-vector entry, one per sentence
PageRank with a weight coefficient w_ij on each edge between sentence vertices

from scipy.sparse.linalg import svds
def low_rank_svd(matrix, singular_count=2):
    u, s, vt = svds(matrix, k=singular_count)
    return u, s, vt

min_sigma_value = max(s) * sv_threshold
s[s < min_sigma_value] = 0
salience_scores = np.sqrt(np.dot(np.square(s), np.square(vt)))

scores = networkx.pagerank(similarity_graph)
ranked_sentences = sorted(((score, index) for index, score in scores.items()), reverse=True)
